props.title: Hustler White

sections.content: Hustler White (1996) stands as a provocative landmark in New Queer Cinema, directed by Bruce LaBruce and Rick Castro. This experimental film follows Mike (Tony Ward), a sex worker on Santa Monica Boulevard, through a darkly comic exploration of LA's hustler subculture. It deliberately references Sunset Boulevard (1950), replacing Hollywood glamour with gritty underground reality. The film's pseudo-documentary style and unflinching approach places it alongside other boundary-pushing 90s queer works like Poison (1991) and The Living End (1992).

sections.content: The mid-90s marked a crucial moment for independent queer cinema breaking into wider consciousness. While Go Fish (1994) and The Watermelon Woman (1996) explored lesbian narratives, films like Hustler White deliberately provoked mainstream sensibilities. LaBruce's punk aesthetic and Castro's photography background created a unique visual style that influenced later queer underground filmmakers like Shortbus (2006) director John Cameron Mitchell. SUBHEAD: The LA Underground Scene on Film

Los Angeles's underbelly has fascinated filmmakers for decades, from Midnight Cowboy (1969) to Tangerine (2015). Hustler White fits into this tradition while subverting it, using experimental techniques and dark humor to challenge audience expectations. The film's influence can be seen in later works exploring marginalized LA communities like L.A. Zombie (2010) and elements of Under the Silver Lake (2018).
